notes: Actual general-fund results for the fiscal year ended June 30, 2025, as reported to the MA Division of Local Services on Schedule A, not a budget.

Includes public schools. Massachusetts cities and towns pay for their schools, and their share of any regional school district, from the general fund, where many other states have separate school districts, so spending and property tax per resident run higher than in those states. Schools are left out of the services and overhead shares.
Intergovernmental assessments are state and county charges deducted from state aid, mostly charter school tuition and school choice, plus transit and county charges. They are counted with schools.

Fixed costs ($17,002,965: health insurance, pensions and other benefits, including for school staff) and other expenditures ($9,800) are spread across departments, including schools, in proportion to their size. Debt service is left out of that spread.

Property tax is the certified tax levy ($42,241,509). The rest of the taxes on Schedule A ($2,531,251) is shown as other taxes and excises: motor vehicle excise, local-option meals and room excises, and penalties and interest. Taxes collected in a year can differ slightly from the levy, so this split is close but not exact.
Covers the general fund. Water, sewer and other enterprise funds, and regional school districts and other separate authorities, are not included.
Left out: other financing sources such as bond proceeds ($0) and transfers from the town's own funds ($1,115,172), which are not new revenue.

Political money counts contributions from PACs and unions to 2 candidates for mayor who file with the MA Office of Campaign and Political Finance, since 2023. Business and corporate contributions to candidates are banned in Massachusetts. Individual donors ($37,759 in the same period) and party and candidate committees are not counted. City council candidates here file with the city clerk, so their money is not included.
